name: NPUs and TPUs
blurb: Purpose-built accelerators outside the GPU line.

items.name: Neural Engine (M-series)
items.note: The NPU in every Apple SoC; the M4 announcement is the canonical spec source for its 38 TOPS on-device engine

items.name: Inferentia
items.note: Amazon's inference-side accelerator, the serving counterpart to Trainium

items.name: Trainium
items.note: Amazon's training chip; Trainium2 UltraServers underpin Anthropic's Project Rainier build-out

items.name: WSE-3
items.note: Wafer-scale engine: one 46,000mm2 die instead of a GPU cluster; 4 trillion transistors

items.name: TPU (Cloud TPU)
items.note: Google's in-house tensor processor family, from Trillium (v6e) onward; trains and serves Gemini and is rentable via Google Cloud

items.name: LPU
items.note: Deterministic single-core-style inference processor; the speed behind the Groq API tracked in the API directory

items.name: Maia 100
items.note: Azure's first in-house AI accelerator, announced with the Cobalt CPU for first-party workloads

reading.body:
Every major cloud provider and several specialists have now built their own silicon rather than relying on GPU vendors, and that consolidation of chip design in-house is the defining structural shift this data captures.

The seven accelerators here split across three functions: training, inference, and on-device execution. AWS separates those first two roles explicitly, with Trainium handling training and Inferentia handling serving. Google's TPU family spans both. Apple's Neural Engine targets neither cloud workload but instead moves inference onto the SoC itself, eliminating the network hop to a data center. Cerebras takes the opposite extreme, replacing a cluster of chips with a single wafer-scale die of 4 trillion transistors. Groq's LPU is optimized for deterministic low-latency inference rather than raw throughput. Microsoft's Maia 100 is the newest entrant among the hyperscalers, paired with a custom CPU for first-party workloads on Azure.

The compute-to-buildings connection is present but indirect here. Custom silicon affects how much physical space and power a given workload consumes, because purpose-built chips can, in principle, do more per watt than general-purpose alternatives. Trainium2 is specifically noted as underpinning Anthropic's Project Rainier build-out, which links chip choice directly to the scale of a data center deployment. The data does not include power figures, rack density, or facility requirements for any of these chips, so the infrastructure consequences cannot be quantified from what is recorded here.
